consensus_summary: Christian consensus identifies the Sabbath day primarily as a type/symbol of spiritual rest in Christ and the eschatological rest of God’s people, grounded in creation rest and anchored by Hebrews 3–4 and Colossians 2:16–17, with secondary readings as covenant sign, redemption memorial, Sunday transfer, literal seventh-day obligation, or millennial typology.
book_summary: The book identifies yom ha-shabbat as the marked member of the sabbath-unit (parallel to the renewed-moon day as day of the month), distinguished from the resting member itself denoted by the doubled phrase shabbat shabbaton wherever that rest falls.
consensus_core_identification: Typological symbol of rest fulfilled in Christ and consummated eschatologically.
book_core_identification: Marked calendrical member of the sabbath-unit (linguistic/structural designation parallel to new-moon day).
boundary_disagreement: Consensus boundaries concern which rest (creation/Christ/eschaton) or which practice (Saturday/Sunday/none) counts; the book’s boundary is internal to biblical usage—when the phrase marks the unit-member versus when doubled language marks the rest itself—without engaging the symbolic or obligatory cases.
material_contradiction: None direct; the book does not assert or deny the rest-in-Christ typology, but replaces the entire symbolic referent with a structural-linguistic one absent from consensus.
rationale: Reducing both to minimum cores shows no shared referent: consensus cores are christological/eschatological rest symbolism (and listed alternatives stay within covenant, liberation, calendrical-obligation, or millennial frames). The book’s core is a technical designation of the term as the marked day-member of a sabbath unit, illustrated by the Ezek 46:1 genitive parallel and the shabbat/shabbat shabbaton distinction. No consensus primary or alternative covers this identification, yielding NOVEL rather than contradiction of an equivalent core.
strongest_objection: One could argue the book is merely clarifying Hebrew/Greek phrasing presupposed by all readings and therefore not a competing ‘meaning,’ but the entry presents this structural marked-member claim as the term’s identification, which consensus never states.
